title: Lutherans and the Reformed
hookLine: Lutherans kept much liturgy; Calvin's Reformed churches stressed God's sovereignty and scripture

lines: WHITE WALLS, A PULPIT, A BIBLE.
cards: The first, a Lutheran church in Germany: an altar with candles, a crucifix, maybe painted panels, a pastor in robes, and up in the balcony an organ roaring out a hymn the whole congregation knows by heart.
Johann Sebastian Bach will one day write music for churches like this. The second, a Reformed church in the Netherlands or Scotland. Whitewashed walls.
No statues, no pictures. In the center, instead of an altar, a tall pulpit, and on it an open Bible. The people sing psalms, plainly.

teach.b: Lutherans follow Martin Luther, whose rule of thumb was: keep whatever in the old worship the Bible doesn't forbid. So they kept much of the liturgy, the church year, vestments, candles, and poured their faith into music.
Bach, a Lutheran, often wrote three letters at the end of his scores: S.D.G., soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory.
The Reformed tradition comes from Swiss reformers, Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich and, above all, John Calvin in Geneva.

teach.h: REFORMED: KEEP WHAT SCRIPTURE CALLS FOR.
teach.b: Their rule went further: in worship, keep what scripture calls for, and let the rest go. Hence the white walls.
From Geneva the Reformed faith spread to Scotland, where John Knox founded what became the Presbyterian church, to the Netherlands, Hungary, and later New England.
At its center is the sovereignty of God: God is king over everything, every life, every hour, and salvation is God's work from start to finish.

A 1647 catechism for Reformed churches in England and Scotland opens well known for it,: "What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever." Notice the second half. Enjoy.
The two families agreed on almost everything, grace, faith, scripture, but split over communion.
At Marburg in 1529, Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen points out of fifteen. The fifteenth was the Lord's Supper.

teach.h: TO GLORIFY GOD, AND TO ENJOY HIM FOR EVER.
teach.b: Luther held that Christ's body is truly present in the bread; Zwingli saw it as a memorial; Calvin later taught a real but spiritual presence. They parted.
Nearly five centuries later, many Lutheran and Reformed churches entered full communion by agreement, in Europe in 1973 and the United States in 1997.

how: Lutheran churches usually worship with a set liturgy, hymns and weekly or frequent communion; Reformed and Presbyterian churches center worship on the reading and preaching of scripture, often in plain sanctuaries.

practice: Picture a church you know, a candle, a window, a plain wooden table, an open Bible, or the room you're in, and find one simple thing that is beautiful exactly as it is. Let it be enough.
If you pray, give it back with Bach's three letters, to God alone the glory; if not, enjoy it, and the catechism would say that counts too.

wordCard.voice: Chief end. The Westminster catechism's phrase for why we exist at all: to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.
